summary:
I've been putting a Japanese-learning app together for myself, called Keikochō, and most of what I've built lately has been about art pipelines and voice more than grammar content. The one that took the longest to track down: a whole batch of AI-generated card images went out looking wrong — washed-out colors, wrong mood — and it turned out the style instructions I thought I was sending to the image model never actually reached it on one of the two rendering paths. Once I found that, a bunch of earlier "casting fights" (getting the right age, gender, expression for a character) made a lot more sense — I'd been fighting the model with prompt tweaks when the real bug was upstream.

I also gave the app fourteen distinct character voices instead of the two or three it had been reusing, mixing a Japanese TTS engine with a commercial voice API for characters the mix couldn't cover well (elderly women, kids). The tricky constraint was that one of those voice engines has no way to check what it's about to say before it says it — the other one does, which matters a lot when a wrong pronunciation teaches the user the wrong word. I ended up scoping the riskier engine to conversational chit-chat only, where a mispronunciation doesn't get memorized as a vocabulary answer.

Most recently I flipped the default interaction in the conversation practice mode from picking a written response to speaking one out loud, with the text still visible so it's imitation rather than pure recall. The interesting part was a Safari quirk on iPhone: if you play audio for the user to imitate while the microphone is already armed to record, the mic silently produces empty recordings — no error, just nothing captured. Fixed it by patching audio playback globally so any playback releases the mic first.

On the infrastructure side, I run a handful of personal services (a budget tracker, a home automation agent) behind Cloudflare tunnels and Tailscale, and I recently chased down a case where a browser-based tool integration kept silently dropping requests — turned out the browser was resolving the tool server directly rather than going through my reverse proxy, which triggers a cascade of CORS problems that mostly fail quietly. The fix was routing everything same-origin instead of trying to patch each CORS header individually.

highlights.oneLiner: Tracked down a style-prompt path that never reached the image model, explaining prior casting fights.
Fixed a browser tool integration silently dropping requests by routing same-origin instead of patching CORS headers.
